title: H-1B Crackdown Drives Tech Talent Back to India as US Companies Expand Offshore Hiring
excerpt: The $100,000 H-1B visa fee and restrictive policies are accelerating a structural shift in global talent flows, with India's tech ecosystem absorbing skilled professionals who once sought American careers.
body:
• India's tech hiring surged 40% above pre-pandemic levels while advanced economies including the U.S. saw a 23% decline, according to LinkedIn's Labor Market Report.
  • The Trump administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions has pushed 30-40% of Indian students studying in the U.S. to seek jobs back in India.
  • U.S. tech giants — Meta, Apple, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix — collectively added over 32,000 jobs in India during 2025, an 18% year-over-year increase.
  • India's Global Capability Center ecosystem has grown to 1,760 centers employing 1.9 million professionals with $64.6 billion in revenue.

A fundamental reversal in global technology talent flows is underway. Restrictive H-1B visa policies and India's rapidly maturing tech ecosystem are combining to redirect skilled professionals away from U.S. careers, reshaping how American enterprises access talent and threatening the country's competitive edge in innovation.

Workforce data from LinkedIn's Labor Market Report shows India's hiring surged 40% above pre-pandemic levels, while advanced economies including the U.S. saw hiring decline by 23%. Companies headquartered in the U.S., UK, Germany, France, and Australia all increased their share of India-based hiring between 2015 and 2025.

The $100,000 Fee That Changed the Calculus

The Trump administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions in September 2025 has fundamentally altered career calculations for engineering talent. India accounted for 71% of approved H-1B beneficiaries last year, with China a distant second at 11.7%, according to U.S. government data.

The fee forced major IT firms with clients such as Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, Meta, and Google to pause onshore rotations, accelerate offshore delivery, and ramp up hiring of U.S. citizens and green card holders.

"The 'American Dream' for aspiring workers will be tough."

— Ganesh Natarajan, Former CEO, Zensar Technologies

Indian Students Reverse Course

The shift is visible at the ground level. Shalu Bindlish, director at Advaita Bedanta Consultants, an India-based talent recruitment agency, said the reversal became evident in recent months. "We have seen Indian tech talents looking for jobs in India rather than moving to the US, and many Indians graduated from US universities applying for jobs in India, which was unprecedented," Bindlish said. "Now we are seeing 30-40 percent of students are keen for Indian jobs after studying in the US."

LinkedIn's data reinforces this: AI engineering talent is eight times more likely to migrate across borders than average professionals, with India serving as a net exporter. But visa restrictions are constraining U.S. talent attraction, pushing American companies to establish operations where talent increasingly chooses to remain.

Big Tech Goes to India

Recognizing the talent shift, American technology giants significantly expanded their Indian operations. Meta, Apple, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix collectively added over 32,000 jobs in India during 2025, representing 18% year-over-year growth, according to staffing firm Xpheno.

For the first time, the top four H-1B approvals for new employment went exclusively to U.S. companies: Amazon with 4,644 approvals, Meta with 1,555, Microsoft with 1,394, and Google with 1,050, according to NFAP analysis.

Wall Street is following the same path. JPMorgan Chase is hiring credit support specialists in Bengaluru, Goldman Sachs is seeking associates to review loans, KKR is adding staff to review portfolio companies, and Millennium Management is recruiting risk analysts for derivatives trading, Bloomberg reported.

India's GCC Ecosystem Steps Up

India's Global Capability Center ecosystem reached 1,760 centers employing more than 1.9 million professionals and generating $64.6 billion in revenue by the end of 2025, according to Zinnov's India GCC Landscape Report. Projections show the ecosystem reaching 2,100 to 2,200 centers employing up to 2.8 million workers by 2030.

"The idea that talent must physically move to headquarters to create value is steadily losing relevance. Capability, not proximity to headquarters, now determines where leadership sits."

— Pari Natarajan, CEO, Zinnov

A Structural Shift, Not a Blip

Industry analysts describe this as a permanent structural change rather than a temporary visa-led adjustment. "Persistent talent shortages in the US and Europe, combined with strong cost advantages, make India increasingly attractive," said Prashray Kala, partner at Everest Group. "India offers deep and scalable next-generation skills across digital, AI, and product roles."

Bringing a mid-level engineer to the U.S. now costs approximately $250,000 per person, including salary, visa fees, and relocation, according to Greyhound Research. The same headcount in India costs one-fifth to one-sixth of that amount.

What's Next

The $100,000 H-1B fee could face legal challenges, but its immediate effect is already locked in. Industry body Nasscom warned the move would "potentially have ripple effects on America's innovation ecosystem." For Indian IT services firms — Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra — the $283 billion sector must overhaul decades-old strategies of rotating talent into U.S. projects. For Indian professionals weighing their options, the calculus has shifted decisively toward staying home.
nri_angle: The H-1B crackdown directly impacts hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the U.S., reshaping career paths and forcing a rethink of the traditional immigration-to-career pipeline that has defined the Indian diaspora experience for decades.
author: Diaspora Desk
